body_markdown:
As I sat with my brothers on the top tier of the grandstands at Watkins Glen during this year’s Hilliard Vintage Grand Prix, the Jaguars, Lotuses, Corvettes, and Mustangs whipping through the corner before us took me back. I remembered when I was a kid watching silent, flickering home movies of my dad driving a Porsche Speedster around tracks like Watkins Glen, Vineland, and Lime Rock in the 1950s and early ‘60s.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


His driving skills were evidently about as good as his parenting skills. He didn’t win many trophies. As a kid, though, I was transfixed by those washed-out grainy old films. His amateur racing career—my parents were both doctors—ended in a bone-crushing crash before I was born. As the youngest of his 11 children, I read the car magazines he left around the house. My older brothers picked up the tools he left in the garage and started fixing and modifying cars on their own.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Ten years ago, my brothers invited me to join them to take in some of the thrills and noise I’d missed. My eldest brother, Andy, drove to Watkins Glen in his red 1964 Porsche 356C; my brother Mark came from Ohio with his son, Jonathan, in his 1964 Triumph TR4; and Carlos came from Virginia in his British Racing Green 1960 TR3. I was a full-time auto journalist then, and I drove in from New York City in a Miata-based Fiat Spider on loan from Fiat Chrysler. It had the right feel. My brother Dan, who never did find cars terribly exciting but liked the idea of hanging out with his brothers, rode in with Andy in the Porsche.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


One night, the six of us were sitting around a hotel room, sipping whiskey and reflecting back on the weekend. We’d watched races, wandered through car shows, and even took part in the parade of classic cars down Watkins Glen’s main street. We also talked a lot. It wasn’t like we all knew each other well. Given the size of our family, there was a generational age spread between my oldest brother and me.


That trip was so much fun that my brothers decided to do it every year. Life’s been busy, and I haven’t joined every year, but they’ve gone to different places like Pittsburgh, West Virginia, Mid-Ohio and Put-In-Bay, with the trips almost always centered around watching vintage races. The group has grown a bit, and some traditions have formed. We have team t-shirts: Bro 1, then Bro 3, Bro 4, 5, and 6. As we tour the paddocks on race days, people ask, “Where’s Bro 2?” He has a shirt, too, but he lives on the west coast and doesn’t join us.


My nephew, Jonathan, got his own shirt, Bro 4.1. When Carlos’s son-in-law started coming and added his Triumph MGC GT to the group, we added Bro 3.1a.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


No more hotel rooms these days. Instead, we rent a house. We take turns making dinner and, always, one night is Cuban black beans and rice served with scrapple, a Pennsylvania Dutch mystery-pork product. It was a childhood favorite created when our mother, of Pennsylvania Dutch descent, tried to incorporate foods our Cuban father liked. We have it at least one night on each trip.


For a few days, the little property feels almost like the 40-room former mansion we grew up in. (It still had all the rooms but lacked the staff.) In the kitchen of our rental house, we jostle with each other getting breakfast in the morning and crash out in front of the living room TV at night just like decades ago.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Peter Valdes-Dapena


This year, I rode to Watkins Glen with my brother Carlos in his 1970 Triumph TR6 and my nephew-in-law Tim Delp, who drove his 1968 MGC GT carrying my luggage in its capacious hatchback. Andy and Dan arrived first in Andy’s 2018 Jaguar F-Pace SUV. That comfortable, modern choice was because Andy’s 1964 Jaguar Mark II was in the midst of an auction sale. The cash he ultimately netted from it will be spent on his next “fun car.”


Mark and his son Jonathan, Bro 4.1, arrived a bit later, having driven all the way from Toledo in Mark’s red 1964 Triumph TR4.


My brothers Andy and Mark represent two opposite types in the world of vintage car ownership. Andy is the serial owner who gets a car, fixes it up, then sells it when he’s done everything he wants with it, like with the Mark II. We tried to make a list of every car Andy’s owned going back more than half a century to when models like a Jaguar E-Type were just interesting used cars. It all started with a pale blue 1964 Triumph Spitfire he bought six months before he got his driver’s license. Dad covered half the $600 price tag. Andy was ready when the driving test came because our house had a driveway circling the property. He practiced driving his Spitfire in circles, NASCAR-style. (He also turned it around the other way to practice turning right.) Later there were cars like an MG TF, a Morgan, a Fiat 124 Sport Coupe and, more recently, a Porsche 911 and that Porsche 356 he drove on our first trip a decade ago.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Mark, on the other hand, has owned, driven, and worked on his red TR4 for nearly thirty years. Back in 1997, his wife presented him with a newspaper classified ad. For $1000, he bought the car as a bunch of disconnected parts, a project left unfinished by a man incapacitated by Lou Gehrig’s disease. Before Mark took the chassis and all the parts, he went inside the house to meet the man who had started the work. “I just want to tell you what you started, I will finish, and I’ll make you proud of what you started,” Mark told him. “It will be done well.”


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Mark got it back together and running in only about eight months, but it was, he admits, not really properly done. Brake issues after six or seven years led to the car being packed away in the garage. It stayed there for years more until his wife gave him, as a Christmas present, a beautiful teak TR4 dashboard.


It came with an ultimatum.


“You need to put that car back on the road,” he recalls her telling him, “and you can’t put it back on the road until it’s worthy of this.”


Peter Valdes-Dapena


He went back into the garage, and, with his son’s help, he did the job right. He taught himself to weld and picked up parts at a local auto graveyard that had an “Everything you can carry in your arms for $25” event a couple of times a year. Now, many years and a new engine later, the little red sports car is as much a part of his life as the house he lives in. It’s impossible to imagine him in anything else.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Andy pulled Carlos into the vintage car scene. Andy had seen how our sisters took trips together, and he got the idea to take road trips with his brothers in their classic cars. He figured the best way to get Carlos involved was to get him a car, so he bought a 1960 Triumph TR3 in fairly rough shape, cleaned it out, fixed it up, and sold it to Carlos at cost.


Carlos loved that car and drove it on that first brothers’ trip to Watkins Glen back in 2016. After a few years, he wanted something a little more modern. That led to his current car, the cream-colored 1970 TR6 he drove on our return to Watkins Glen this year.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


Carlos’s son-in-law, Tim Delp, decided these trips sounded like a blast. After joining us on a visit to the Pittsburgh Vintage Grand Prix, he decided to join the club properly and bought himself a 1968 MGC GT. Soon, that car was joined in Tim’s big garage by Carlos’s TR6 as a permanent resident so the two of them can work on their cars together and drive together to the “Bro Trips.”


Before we went to watch the races this year, we had a drive of our own to do. We’d missed registering for any of the tours that were offered that weekend, but I had planned out a route just for us. Tops down, we drove long straight roads past farm silos, then twisting roads through the hills and gentle curves down the shore of Keuka Lake.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


For a while, I rode in Mark’s TR4 as the lead car in the group. He offered to let me drive, but I demurred—I’d designed this route for my brothers to enjoy in their cars. I wanted him to have the experience, and he loved it with the breeze coming in off the lake and glimpses of still water through the trees. We stopped and took in Glenn H. Curtiss Museum’s airplanes, cars, and motorcycles before heading back.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


We spent the next couple of days at Watkins Glen, watching the cars on the track in races that were often surprisingly close and competitive. Even more fun was walking through the paddock, getting close to the cars before and after the races.


Peter Valdes-Dapena


We marveled at the finish on a polished aluminum 1961 Aston Martin DB4 Zagato that, to our surprise, raced that afternoon. We thought no one would risk that body in actual competition, but there it was! We had also watched a 1955 Corvette get some body damage cut away and then duke it out in the same race as the Aston.


It was an amazing, exciting weekend as they always are. Next year, I think we’ll be heading to some winding roads in southern Ohio. We’re working on a logo design for hats to go with our shirts. No one’s going to miss us.


Peter Valdes-Dapena
